cards.t: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: when no surgical biopsy is needed
q: when can idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis be diagnosed without a lung biopsy
what are the four criteria for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
how confident is a diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis without biopsy
cards.x:
In a patient over 65, a surgical lung biopsy is not needed when four criteria are all met:

- Idiopathic disease by history, with inspiratory crackles on examination.
- Restrictive physiology on pulmonary function testing.
- Radiographic evidence of progressive fibrosis over several years.
- Diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing on high-resolution computed tomography.

When all four are present the diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis carries about 90% confidence, which is why the biopsy can be skipped. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the most common subtype of idiopathic interstitial pneumonia.

cards.t: Sleep versus coma (how to tell them apart)
q: what is the difference between sleep and coma
how do you tell sleep from coma
is sleep a form of unconsciousness
cards.x:
Sleep and coma are both forms of unconsciousness, and the one big difference is whether the person can be brought back. Sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sensory stimuli or other stimuli. Coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused by stimuli.

So a person who is unconscious, then roused by a loud voice and a squeeze of the shoulder, and who goes on to answer questions, was asleep, even if a quieter stimulus failed first. Someone who does not rouse to any stimulus points to coma.

Sleep is also just one of many states of brain activity, alongside wakefulness, extreme excitement and different moods such as exhilaration, depression and fear. These states arise mostly from activating or inhibiting forces generated within the brain.

cards.t: Sleep cycles and stages across a night
k: how many sleep cycles per night
q: how long is a sleep cycle
what are the stages of sleep
when does deep sleep happen during the night
how does REM change over the night
cards.x:
A night of sleep averages about 8 hours and contains 4 to 5 separate sleep cycles, each lasting 90 to 120 minutes. Every cycle swings between two types of sleep: slow-wave sleep, also called non-rapid eye movement sleep, which is deep and restful, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which is not restful or deep.

Non-REM is divided into three stages: stage one (N1), stage two (N2) and stage three (N3). N2 makes up the majority of the sleep cycle. REM is simply REM, with no stages.

The pattern across the night: sleep descends to its deepest stage within the first hour, and that deepest stage appears only in the early cycles. REM periods come back about every 90 minutes and grow longer toward morning.

cards.t: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep: timing and features
q: what is REM sleep
how long does REM sleep last
what happens to the body in REM sleep
why is REM sleep called active sleep
cards.x:
Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is the active, dreaming form of sleep. It comes in episodes that make up about 25% of a young adult's sleep time. Each episode recurs about every 90 minutes and lasts 5 to 30 minutes.

During REM the brain is very active and dreams are vivid. Heart rate and breathing become irregular, and brain metabolism can rise by as much as 20%. The sleeper is not fully aware of the surroundings, and is harder to arouse by sensory stimuli than in non-REM sleep, yet people can wake spontaneously in the morning out of REM. It is not the most restful sleep.

The episodes depend on how tired you are: when a person is extremely sleepy, each REM episode is short or even absent, and as the person becomes more rested the episodes lengthen. That is why REM gets longer later in the night.

cards.t: Muscle atonia in REM sleep
k: why muscles go limp in REM
q: why are muscles paralyzed during REM sleep
which muscles keep working in REM sleep
why do the eyes move in REM sleep
cards.x:
In rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, muscle tone is very depressed. This is atonia: the voluntary muscles go limp because the spinal muscle control areas are inhibited, specifically the alpha motor neurons, the nerves that drive the muscles. An electromyogram, the muscle trace, shows this inactivity.

Two sets of muscles are spared: the eye muscles and the diaphragm. Because the eye muscles escape the atonia, the eyes keep moving, which gives REM its rapid, irregular, sharply peaked eye movements on an electrooculogram (the eye-movement trace). The brain waves of REM look much like waking, so atonia is a useful clue that the sleeper is in REM.

cards.t: Why REM is called paradoxical or desynchronized sleep
q: why is REM sleep called paradoxical sleep
what does desynchronized sleep mean
why does REM look like being awake on an EEG
cards.x:
Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is called paradoxical because the sleeper looks asleep while the electroencephalogram (EEG, the brain-wave tracing) looks like wakefulness. It is also called desynchronized sleep, because neurons are not firing in step with one another. The result is a tracing that is irregular and high frequency, much like the tracing of an awake, active person.

That is why REM is often hard to tell apart from alert wakefulness on the brain waves alone. One body clue that it is REM: the voluntary muscles show atonia (they go limp), except the eyes and the diaphragm.

cards.t: Non-REM (slow-wave) sleep
q: what happens in non-REM sleep
why is slow-wave sleep so restful
do dreams happen in non-REM sleep
what is the first hour of sleep like after being up all night
cards.x:
Slow-wave sleep is the deep, extremely restful kind of sleep, the counterpart of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. It is also called non-REM sleep. The deep sleep you fall into in the first hour after being awake for more than 24 hours is this type.

The body winds down: peripheral vascular tone and other vegetative functions decrease, with a 10 to 30% fall in blood pressure, heart rate, breathing rate and metabolic rate. Parasympathetic tone increases, and blood pressure is low, the heart rate is slow and breathing is slower.

It is often called the dreamless state, but that is not always accurate: dreams and nightmares do occur in non-REM sleep. They are less vivid than dreams in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, with less bodily muscle activity, and they are often not remembered because they are not consolidated in memory.

cards.t: REM versus non-REM sleep: side-by-side comparison
q: what is the difference between REM and non-REM sleep
which type of sleep is more restful
how do heart rate and breathing differ in REM and non-REM sleep
cards.x:
The two types of sleep, slow-wave (non-rapid eye movement) sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, are close to opposites in how the body behaves:

- Restfulness and dreams: non-REM is deep and extremely restful, with less vivid dreams that are often not remembered. REM is not restful or deep, with vivid dreams and bodily muscle activity.
- Body rates: non-REM brings increased parasympathetic tone and a 10 to 30% fall in blood pressure, heart rate, breathing and metabolism. In REM, heart rate and breathing become irregular and brain metabolism rises by as much as 20%.
- Muscles: in REM, tone is very depressed (atonia except the eyes and diaphragm), with rapid, irregular eye movements.
- Arousal: stage three (N3) is the hardest non-REM stage to arouse; REM is harder to arouse by sensory stimuli than non-REM, yet spontaneous morning waking can occur.
- Brain waves: non-REM slows progressively to delta waves; REM looks like wakefulness.

cards.t: Why sleep matters: the functions of sleep
q: why is sleep important
what are the physiological functions of sleep
what happens if you restrict sleep for a few days
cards.x:
Why we need sleep is not fully understood: researchers have a limited understanding of it, and its specific physiological functions remain a mystery that is still being researched. What is known is that sleep restriction over a few days can decrease a person's cognitive and physical performance, overall productivity and health.

The effects fall into two major groups: effects on the nervous system and effects on other functional systems of the body. Proposed functions include:

- neural maturation
- helping learning and memory
- targeted erasure of synapses, so unimportant information does not clutter the network of connections
- cognition
- clearing metabolic waste products made by neural activity in the awake brain
- conserving metabolic energy

cards.t: The cycle between sleep and wakefulness
q: how does the brain switch between wake and sleep
why do we get sleepy after being awake for hours
what keeps us awake
cards.x:
There is no definitive explanation of the sleep-wakefulness cycle, only proposed theories. The theory runs like this.

When the sleep centers are not active, the reticular activating nuclei in the mesencephalon (midbrain) and upper pons are released from inhibition and switch on by themselves. They excite the cerebral cortex and the peripheral nervous system, which send positive feedback signals back to the same nuclei, so wakefulness keeps itself going.

After many hours of activity, the neurons of this activating system become fatigued. The positive feedback cycle between the midbrain nuclei and the cortex fades, and the sleep-promoting centers take over. That is the switch from wakefulness to sleep.

cards.t: The four waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha, beta, theta, delta
q: what are the four brain waves on an EEG
what is the difference between alpha and beta waves
when do delta waves occur
what are theta waves
cards.x:
The electroencephalogram (EEG) records brain electrical activity, and its pattern depends on how excited different parts of the brain are in sleep, wakefulness or brain disorders such as epilepsy or psychosis. The four normal waves, from fastest to slowest:

- Beta: faster than 14 cycles per second, up to 80. Asynchronous and low voltage, seen mainly over the parietal and frontal regions when the person is awake, alert and actively processing information.
- Alpha: 8 to 13 cycles per second and rhythmical. Present in almost all healthy awake adults who are quiet and resting; most intense over the occipital region; disappears in deep sleep.
- Theta: 4 to 7 cycles per second. Seen in children, in some adults under emotional stress such as disappointment and frustration, and in many brain disorders, especially degenerative ones.
- Delta: slower than 3.5 cycles per second, with voltages 2 to 4 times greater than most other waves. Seen in very deep sleep, infancy and serious organic brain disease.

cards.t: Why alpha waves give way to beta waves
q: why do alpha waves disappear when you open your eyes
what replaces alpha waves when you concentrate
what happens to the EEG when attention is directed
cards.x:
Alpha waves belong to a quiet, resting brain, so they vanish when the brain goes to work. When an awake person's attention is directed to a specific mental activity, the alpha waves stop and are replaced by faster beta waves. The same thing happens on a tracing when the eyes open: alpha disappears, and when the eyes close it returns.

So awake with eyes closed and relaxed gives alpha, and awake with eyes open and alert gives beta.

cards.t: Stage N3: deep sleep and delta waves
q: what is stage N3 sleep
what brain waves are in deep sleep
what happens during stage N3
what happens to deep sleep with age
cards.x:
Stage three (N3), also called deep sleep or slow-wave sleep, is the deepest stage of non-rapid eye movement sleep. It is restful sleep, and it is more difficult to arouse a person from it than from the other non-rapid eye movement stages.

Its brain-wave signature is the delta wave: a wave slower than 3.5 cycles per second with high voltage. Body and tissue growth and repair occur during this stage. N3 decreases with age.

cards.t: EEG changes across wakefulness and sleep stages
k: brain waves in each sleep stage
waves in N1 N2 N3 REM
alpha beta theta delta by stage
q: which brain waves appear in each stage of sleep
what does the EEG look like in REM sleep
how do brain waves change as sleep deepens
cards.x:
As a person goes from awake to deep asleep, the electroencephalogram (EEG) slows and the waves grow taller:

- Awake, eyes open (alert and active): beta.
- Awake, eyes closed (relaxed): alpha.
- Stage one (N1), the drowsy transition from wakefulness and light sleep: theta.
- Stage two (N2), less responsive and deeper sleep with a falling heart rate and temperature, and the longest stage by total duration: theta, plus sleep spindles and K complexes.
- Stage three (N3), deep sleep: delta.
- Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep: mixed, low-voltage waves with sawtooth waves, like the awake state (beta) but with atonia.

A memory aid: going down into sleep the waves slow down. Busy is beta, at rest is alpha, tired is theta, deep is delta, and then REM jumps back to beta.

cards.t: Sleep spindles and K complexes (stage N2)
q: what are sleep spindles
what are K complexes
what is stage N2 sleep
which EEG findings mark N2
cards.x:
Sleep spindles and K complexes are the special features of stage two (N2) sleep. N2 is less responsive, deeper sleep than the drowsy first stage (N1), with a falling heart rate and body temperature. It is also the longest stage by total duration.

The background waves in N2 are theta waves. On top of them are:

- Sleep spindles: bursts of monomorphic (all alike) waves at 12 to 14 cycles per second.
- K complexes: negative sharp waves followed by a positive component.

cards.t: Apnea versus hypopnea
q: what is the difference between apnea and hypopnea
how is an apnea defined
how long does an apnea last
cards.x:
Apnea and hypopnea are the two kinds of breathing events counted in sleep-disordered breathing, and the difference is how far breathing drops.

An apnea is near or total cessation of breathing: a decrease in airflow of 90% or more, measured by a thermistor, lasting at least 10 seconds.

A hypopnea is milder: slowed, shallow, restricted breathing in episodes of 10 seconds or longer, happening repeatedly during sleep.

Quick way to remember it: an apnea is breathing that (nearly) stops, and a hypopnea is breathing that stays on but gets slow and shallow. Both last 10 seconds or longer.

cards.t: Obstructive, central and mixed apnea: how they differ
q: what is the difference between obstructive and central sleep apnea
what is mixed sleep apnea
what are the types of sleep-disordered breathing
cards.x:
Sleep-disordered breathing is divided into obstructive sleep apnea, central sleep apnea and sleep-related hypoventilation. For the apnea types, the airflow stops in every case. What tells them apart is whether the person is still trying to breathe, which is called respiratory effort:

- Obstructive: no airflow, but effort continues. The airway collapses while the patient still tries to breathe.
- Central: no airflow and no effort at all.
- Mixed: no airflow, and effort is absent in the first part of the event and resumes in the latter part.

So obstructive is a blocked pipe with the person still pushing, and central is no push at all.

cards.t: Obstructive sleep apnea: who gets it and why
q: what causes obstructive sleep apnea
what are the risk factors for obstructive sleep apnea
how common is obstructive sleep apnea
what neck size is a risk factor for sleep apnea
cards.x:
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is the most common form of sleep-disordered breathing. It is caused by narrowing of the upper airway from excessive soft tissue or structural abnormalities. Its prevalence increases with age, and it is more prevalent in post-menopausal than premenopausal women.

The risk factors mostly fit that cause:

- Obesity, macroglossia (a large tongue), micrognathia (a small jaw), retrognathia (a set-back jaw) and enlarged tonsils.
- A thick neck: a circumference of 17 inches or more in men and 16 in women.
- Increasing age, male more than female, and family history.
- Use of alcohol or sedatives, and conditions such as hypothyroidism.

Enlarged tonsils are both a risk factor and an examination finding.

cards.t: Obstructive sleep apnea: symptoms and examination findings
q: what are the symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea
what does the exam show in obstructive sleep apnea
what history clues point to sleep apnea
cards.x:
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) shows up as a night-time story plus a daytime story.

History: daytime sleepiness, unrefreshing sleep, witnessed apnea (someone sees the breathing stop), awakening with snorting or gasping, loud habitual snoring, morning headaches, nocturia (waking at night to urinate), poorly controlled hypertension, decreased concentration or memory, irritability, decreased libido and nocturnal sweating.

Examination: obesity, macroglossia (a large tongue), micrognathia and retrognathia (a small or set-back jaw), a large neck (around 17 inches in men and 16 in women), enlarged tonsils and a crowded posterior oropharynx (the back of the throat looks tight).

The exam findings are the same things that narrow the upper airway, which is the cause of OSA.

cards.t: Differential diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea
q: what else can look like obstructive sleep apnea
what is on the differential for sleep apnea
which conditions cause nocturnal breathing symptoms like sleep apnea
cards.x:
Several other problems can look like obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), either because they disturb breathing at night or because they cause daytime sleepiness. The differential is:

- Central sleep apnea.
- Nocturnal dyspnea (night-time breathlessness) from congestive heart failure.
- An abnormal swallowing disorder.
- Panic attacks.
- Nocturnal asthma.
- Reflux disease of the esophagus (gastro-esophageal reflux disease).
- Nocturnal seizures.
- Other causes of daytime sleepiness: narcolepsy and periodic limb movement disorder.

The sleep study (polysomnogram) is the gold standard test for OSA.

cards.t: Polysomnogram types: split-night, all-night and titration
q: what is a split-night sleep study
when is an all-night polysomnogram used
what is CPAP titration
what is the gold standard test for sleep apnea
cards.x:
A polysomnogram (an overnight sleep study) is the gold standard for diagnosing obstructive sleep apnea. It comes in a few forms:

- Split-night polysomnogram: the first 2 hours of sleep are recorded to determine severity. If the apnea is significant, the study continues with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) titration, which means finding the exact pressure that keeps the airway open.
- All-night polysomnogram: done if the sleep-disordered breathing is mild to moderate at baseline. It shows severity in different stages of sleep and in different sleep positions.
- Positive airway pressure titration on its own: used when the diagnosis is already known.

Thyroid-stimulating hormone is checked if hypothyroidism is suspected.

cards.t: Home sleep apnea test: what it can and cannot do
k: when to avoid home sleep test
q: when can you use a home sleep apnea test
why might a home sleep test miss sleep apnea
who needs a polysomnogram instead of a home kit
cards.x:
A home testing kit assesses only obstructive sleep apnea, not other sleep disorders. It will not always diagnose mild disease; it is most helpful in moderate to severe disease.

Use a polysomnogram, not a home kit, when the patient has:

- significant cardiopulmonary disease
- neuromuscular weakness
- awake hypoventilation or hypoxemia
- stroke
- long-term opioid use, severe insomnia, or concern for a non-obstructive sleep disorder

A negative home study in someone who still snores and is sleepy therefore needs a polysomnogram, because home kits will not always diagnose mild disease. A polysomnogram can also find other sleep disorders that a home kit cannot assess.

cards.t: Apnea-hypopnea index, respiratory disturbance index and diagnostic criteria
q: how is the apnea-hypopnea index calculated
what is the difference between AHI and RDI
what criteria diagnose obstructive sleep apnea
cards.x:
Both indexes count breathing events per hour of sleep. The apnea-hypopnea index is (apneas + hypopneas) divided by total sleep time in hours. The respiratory disturbance index is (apneas + hypopneas + respiratory effort-related arousals) divided by total sleep time in hours. A respiratory effort-related arousal is an obstructive reduction of the upper airway that is not an apnea or hypopnea. So the second index simply adds those arousals.

Obstructive sleep apnea is confirmed when either criterion is met and the symptoms are not explained by another medical or sleep condition, medication or substance use:

- 5 or more predominantly obstructive respiratory events per hour of sleep plus one symptom: sleepiness, fatigue, insomnia or other symptoms impairing sleep-related quality of life; waking with breath holding, gasping or choking; or habitual snoring or breathing interruptions noted by a bed partner or other observer.
- 15 or more predominantly obstructive respiratory events, with no symptom needed.

cards.t: The STOP-Bang questionnaire: items and when to use it
q: what is STOP-Bang
what are the STOP-Bang questions
is STOP-Bang used to screen the community for sleep apnea
cards.x:
The questionnaire (STOP-Bang) is a screening tool for obstructive sleep apnea, with one point for every yes. Its eight questions spell out its name: Are you a loud Snorer? Are you often Tired, fatigued or sleepy in the daytime? Has anyone Observed you stop breathing or choke or gasp in your sleep? Do you have, or are you treated for, high blood Pressure? Is your body mass index (BMI) more than 35? Are you older than 50 (Age)? Is your Neck (shirt collar) 16 inches / 40 cm or larger? Are you male (Gender)?

Its use is narrow. It has been used before surgery in people with no known diagnosis who may be at risk of perioperative complications, and it has the highest sensitivity of all the questionnaires. But screening questionnaires should not be used routinely to screen the community, and it cannot be an accurate screening tool in people without symptoms.

Note its own cutoffs: neck 16 inches / 40 cm for anyone, not the 17 inch (men) and 16 inch (women) risk-factor numbers.

cards.t: STOP-Bang scoring and risk bands
q: how do you score STOP-Bang
what score is high risk on STOP-Bang
how can someone be high risk on STOP-Bang with a score under 5
cards.x:
Add one point for each yes (maximum 8). The risk of obstructive sleep apnea is then:

- Low: yes to 0 to 2 questions.
- Intermediate: yes to 3 to 4.
- High: yes to 5 to 8.

There is a shortcut into the high-risk group even with a lower total: yes to 2 or more of the first four (STOP) questions plus any one of male gender, body mass index above 35 kg/m2, or neck circumference 16 inches / 40 cm.

Example: someone who snores, is tired and has a body mass index of 38 scores 3, which is intermediate by the count alone. But 2 yes answers to the first four questions plus a body mass index above 35 meet the added rule, so that person is high risk. Watch the cutoffs: body mass index must be more than 35, and age must be older than 50.

cards.t: Obstructive sleep apnea treatment: CPAP, devices and lifestyle
q: what is the most effective treatment for obstructive sleep apnea
when is an oral appliance not effective
what lifestyle changes help sleep apnea
cards.x:
Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the most effective treatment for obstructive sleep apnea. At home it is a mask over the nose, or over the nose and mouth, with a hose to a machine at the bedside. The other non-drug options fit specific patients:

- Autotitrating (adjustable) positive airway pressure: for patients without significant comorbid conditions.
- Positional therapy, if events happen when lying supine: a sleep belt or shirt keeps the patient on their side.
- Oral appliance: not effective in severe disease or if the patient has no teeth.
- Nasal expiratory resistance device: uses the patient's own breathing to make expiratory positive airway pressure.

Risk modification means diet and exercise for weight loss, and avoiding alcohol and other sedatives. Education means referral to a sleep physician and proper counseling.

cards.t: Modafinil, armodafinil and nasal steroids in sleep apnea
q: what are the side effects of modafinil and armodafinil
when do you use caution with modafinil
why use nasal steroids in sleep apnea
cards.x:
The drug options for obstructive sleep apnea are stimulants (modafinil or armodafinil) and nasal steroids.

The stimulants' listed side effects are headache, nervousness or anxiety, dizziness, nausea, and dermatologic and systemic hypersensitivity (so a widespread rash with feeling unwell after starting the drug fits). They have many potential drug interactions. Use caution in patients with cardiovascular, hepatic or psychiatric conditions, and give lower doses in the elderly.

Nasal steroids are for nasal congestion or inflammation from allergic rhinitis.

cards.t: Surgery for obstructive sleep apnea
q: what surgeries treat obstructive sleep apnea
which sleep apnea surgery is a cure
when is surgery used if CPAP is not tolerated
cards.x:
Surgery is for selected patients, and several options are for those who cannot tolerate continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP):

- Radiofrequency ablation: mild to moderate disease in patients who cannot tolerate CPAP.
- Palatal implants: mild disease in patients who cannot tolerate CPAP.
- Maxillomandibular advancement.
- Tracheostomy: a cure, because it bypasses the site of upper airway obstruction.
- Bariatric surgery for weight loss, which may help.

The tracheostomy logic is the useful one to remember: the problem is a blocked upper airway, and a tracheostomy goes around it.

cards.t: Risks of untreated obstructive sleep apnea
q: what happens if obstructive sleep apnea is not treated
how much does sleep apnea raise the risk of sudden cardiac death
how much does sleep apnea raise the risk of car accidents
cards.x:
Untreated obstructive sleep apnea raises the risk of several serious outcomes:

- 2.5 times the driving accidents (more motor vehicle crashes from daytime sleepiness).
- 3 to 6 times the risk of sudden cardiac death at night.
- High mortality from heart failure.
- 3 times the risk of hypertension.
- Pulmonary hypertension, stroke, insulin resistance, arrhythmias and ischemic heart disease.

Increased risk of gout is also listed.

cards.t: How obstructive sleep apnea affects the heart, hormones and inflammation
q: how does sleep apnea affect the cardiovascular system
what hormones change in sleep apnea
does CPAP improve inflammation in sleep apnea
cards.x:
Untreated obstructive sleep apnea has effects well beyond the airway.

Cardiovascular: increased sympathetic (fight-or-flight) tone, bradycardia (a slow heart rate), increased blood pressure variability, increased arrhythmias, and an increased risk of aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection.

Endocrine: C-reactive protein, cortisol and amyloid go up, while growth hormone and prolactin go down.

Immunity: proinflammatory cytokines (inflammation-promoting chemical messengers) increase, and they improve with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).

cards.t: Reflux with obstructive sleep apnea
q: why do people with sleep apnea have reflux
how common is reflux in sleep apnea
does CPAP help reflux in sleep apnea
cards.x: Reflux is very common in obstructive sleep apnea: 75 to 100% of patients have reflux disease of the esophagus or laryngopharyngeal reflux (reflux up to the throat). The reason given is decreased intrathoracic pressure, the pressure inside the chest. Reflux improves with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), so CPAP can help the reflux too.

cards.t: Pulmonary hypertension and obstructive sleep apnea
q: how is sleep apnea linked to pulmonary hypertension
what group of pulmonary hypertension is sleep apnea in
does sleep apnea cause right-sided heart failure
cards.x:
Pulmonary hypertension (high blood pressure in the lung arteries) is one of the complications of untreated obstructive sleep apnea. Obstructive sleep apnea is classified with group 3 pulmonary hypertension, especially when it coexists with obesity hypoventilation syndrome or another cause of daytime hypoxemia (low blood oxygen while awake).

Right-sided heart failure from pulmonary hypertension is also given as a late feature of obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

cards.t: Obstructive sleep apnea, diabetes, metabolic syndrome and fatty liver
q: how is sleep apnea linked to diabetes
does sleep apnea cause fatty liver
what metabolic problems come with sleep apnea
cards.x:
Obstructive sleep apnea is linked to metabolic disease. It increases insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and diabetes complications. Higher glucose and triglycerides are independently associated with it, and it may worsen cardiovascular risk in people with metabolic syndrome.

It is also tied to nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, which is 2 to 3 times as prevalent in obstructive sleep apnea.

cards.t: Central sleep apnea: what it is, causes and risk factors
q: what is central sleep apnea
what causes central sleep apnea
how is central sleep apnea different from obstructive sleep apnea
who gets central sleep apnea
cards.x:
In central sleep apnea the brainstem stops sending signals to breathe, so there is no airflow and no respiratory effort. That is the key contrast with obstructive sleep apnea, where the airway collapses while the patient still tries to breathe.

The mechanism is an increased sensitivity to arterial carbon dioxide, which gives an unstable pattern of hyperventilation alternating with apnea. It is less common than obstructive sleep apnea.

Risk factors: congestive heart failure (especially with Cheyne-Stokes breathing), stroke, opioid medications, hypoxia, high altitude, and using continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).

cards.t: Cheyne-Stokes breathing in heart failure
q: what causes Cheyne-Stokes breathing
why does heart failure cause central sleep apnea
is Cheyne-Stokes breathing protective
cards.x:
Cheyne-Stokes breathing is the pattern especially linked to central sleep apnea in congestive heart failure. It is caused by a prolonged circulation delay between the pulmonary capillaries and the carotid chemoreceptors (the sensors that monitor the blood).

A twist matters for treatment. Cheyne-Stokes breathing can be a protective mechanism, which is one reason adaptive servo-ventilation is not used for every patient, especially in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

cards.t: Central sleep apnea: symptoms and diagnosis
q: what are the symptoms of central sleep apnea
how is central sleep apnea diagnosed
can you diagnose central sleep apnea with a home test
cards.x:
Central sleep apnea looks a lot like obstructive sleep apnea. Patients have insomnia, frequent awakenings, nocturnal dyspnea (breathlessness at night), nonrestorative sleep and daytime sleepiness. Snoring is less common than in obstructive sleep apnea, but the condition sounds very similar.

Diagnosis needs polysomnography; home testing is not sufficient. The finding is repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion, which means no chest or belly movement, matching the absent respiratory effort.

cards.t: Central sleep apnea treatment and adaptive servo-ventilation
q: how is central sleep apnea treated
when is adaptive servo-ventilation used
why avoid adaptive servo-ventilation in heart failure
cards.x:
Central sleep apnea is treated in steps:

- Treat the underlying cause: in heart failure, optimize heart failure therapy; with opioids, reduce the opioids; at high altitude, descend.
- Consider continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) first.
- If CPAP fails, consider adaptive servo-ventilation, a positive airway pressure therapy that monitors breathing in real time and adjusts the pressure.

Adaptive servo-ventilation is not used for all patients, for safety reasons, especially in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. With poor left ventricular function, reducing preload can decrease cardiac output, and Cheyne-Stokes breathing can be a protective mechanism.

cards.t: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (Pickwickian syndrome)
q: what is obesity hypoventilation syndrome
why is obesity hypoventilation a diagnosis of exclusion
what is Pickwickian syndrome
cards.x:
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also called Pickwickian syndrome) is awake alveolar hypoventilation in an obese person: the carbon dioxide in the arterial blood is raised even while awake, because the person is not breathing enough to clear it. It counts only when other conditions that cause alveolar hypoventilation cannot explain it, which makes it a diagnosis of exclusion.

It becomes more likely as body mass index increases, and it is associated with increased cardiovascular illness and death.

cards.t: Risk factors for obesity hypoventilation syndrome
q: what are the risk factors for obesity hypoventilation syndrome
is male sex a risk factor for obesity hypoventilation
at what age does obesity hypoventilation present
cards.x:
Four risk factors are listed for obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS):

- Central obesity, meaning a high waist-to-hip ratio.
- Reduced lung function from obesity.
- Reduced inspiratory muscle strength.
- Severe obstructive sleep apnea.

Male gender is not a risk factor. Patients may present in their 50s and 60s.

cards.t: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome: symptoms and findings
q: what are the symptoms of obesity hypoventilation syndrome
how many patients with obesity hypoventilation also have sleep apnea
what are the late findings of obesity hypoventilation
cards.x:
The symptoms of obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) are not specific. They reflect obesity, coexisting obstructive sleep apnea and complications such as pulmonary hypertension. The typical patient is obese (body mass index over 30) and hypersomnolent (excessively sleepy).

- About 90% have coexisting obstructive sleep apnea symptoms (70% severe): daytime hypersomnolence, loud snoring, choking during sleep, resuscitative snorting, fatigue, impaired concentration and memory, a small oropharynx and a thick neck.
- About 10% have coexisting sleep hypoventilation, with fewer witnessed apneas, in older females.

Many present late with end-stage disease: severe hypoxemic hypercapnic respiratory failure and right-sided heart failure from pulmonary hypertension. Clues include facial plethora (facial swelling, puffiness), elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly and pedal edema.

cards.t: Who to screen for obesity hypoventilation syndrome
q: who should be screened for obesity hypoventilation syndrome
what bicarbonate level suggests obesity hypoventilation
what oxygen saturation prompts screening for obesity hypoventilation
cards.x:
Screen an obese person, with or without obstructive sleep apnea, who has any of these:

- Unexplained awake room-air oxygen saturation of 94% or less, or an overnight lowest saturation below 80%.
- Unexplained dyspnea on exertion.
- Signs of pulmonary hypertension or right-sided heart failure: elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, pedal edema.
- Facial plethora (facial swelling, puffiness).
- A raised bicarbonate on labs.

When suspicion is low to moderate, a serum bicarbonate over 27 means a higher chance of obesity hypoventilation syndrome and the need for an arterial blood gas.

cards.t: Diagnosing obesity hypoventilation syndrome
q: how is obesity hypoventilation syndrome diagnosed
what is the gold standard test for obesity hypoventilation
what arterial carbon dioxide level defines obesity hypoventilation
cards.x:
Diagnosis needs three things together:

- Obesity: body mass index over 30.
- Awake alveolar hypoventilation: arterial carbon dioxide pressure over 45 mm Hg.
- Alternative causes of hypercapnia (raised carbon dioxide) and hypoventilation excluded.

Because it is a diagnosis of exclusion, the workup includes a comprehensive metabolic panel, complete blood count, thyroid function tests, pulmonary function tests, chest film and toxicology screen, plus serum bicarbonate. The gold standard test is polysomnography with continuous nocturnal carbon dioxide monitoring.

cards.t: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome treatment
q: how is obesity hypoventilation syndrome treated
when do you use BiPAP versus CPAP in obesity hypoventilation
what is second-line treatment for obesity hypoventilation
cards.x:
Treatment is multidisciplinary.

First line is a weight loss program plus positive airway pressure, and the type depends on the sleep problem: with coexisting obstructive sleep apnea, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP); with sleep-related hypoventilation, bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP). Lifestyle change (diet, exercise, behavioral change) goes with it.

Second line is for patients who fail or cannot tolerate first line: tracheostomy with nocturnal ventilation is very effective, bariatric surgery may help, and medications are used only for those who fail diet and exercise.

Refer to a sleep specialist and give proper counseling.

cards.t: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome complications and prognosis
q: what are the complications of obesity hypoventilation syndrome
what is the prognosis of obesity hypoventilation
what is the leading cause of death in obesity hypoventilation
cards.x:
Complications include pulmonary hypertension, right-sided heart failure, congestive heart failure, hypertension, insulin resistance and daytime sleepiness.

Morbidity and mortality are high, and the disease tends to progress when untreated, with many patients developing pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death. Patients have higher hospitalization rates and are more likely to need intensive care, intubation or long-term care at discharge. A poor prognosis goes with significant awake hypoxemia at diagnosis and on positive airway pressure therapy.

cards.t: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome versus obstructive sleep apnea
k: difference between sleep apnea and Pickwickian syndrome
q: what is the difference between obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome
can someone have both sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation
when is BiPAP used instead of CPAP in obesity hypoventilation
cards.x:
Obstructive sleep apnea is about the airway collapsing during sleep while the person keeps trying to breathe. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is about not breathing enough while awake: awake alveolar hypoventilation, shown by an arterial carbon dioxide pressure over 45 mm Hg, in an obese person (body mass index over 30) when no other cause explains it.

The two often travel together. About 90% of patients with obesity hypoventilation have coexisting obstructive sleep apnea symptoms (70% severe), and about 10% have coexisting sleep hypoventilation. That split guides the pressure machine: continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) when obstructive sleep apnea is present, and bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) when sleep-related hypoventilation is present.

cards.t: Sleep apnea in older adults
q: how does obstructive sleep apnea differ in older adults
why is sleep apnea mortality lower in the elderly
what changes in medication for elderly sleep apnea patients
cards.x:
In older adults, the prevalence of obstructive sleep apnea increases with age, and obesity hypoventilation often presents in the 50s and 60s.

Mortality from obstructive sleep apnea is lower in the elderly because they compensate. They still have drowsiness and nocturia (waking at night to urinate), and both improve with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).

On drugs, caution is needed with cardiovascular, hepatic and psychiatric disease, and the elderly get lower stimulant doses. Referral is the same as for younger adults: a sleep physician or sleep specialist, with counseling.

cards.t: Interstitial lung disease: what it is
q: what is interstitial lung disease
why does interstitial lung disease cause shortness of breath
is interstitial lung disease cancer or infection
cards.x:
Interstitial lung disease is a broad category of more than 200 disorders that are hard to classify. What they share is scarring (fibrosis) and/or inflammation of the lungs. The target is the parenchyma, the gas-transfer part of the lung (alveoli, alveolar ducts and respiratory bronchioles), where the alveolar walls thicken, fibroblasts multiply, collagen is laid down and, if it goes on, pulmonary fibrosis develops. It is not malignant and not infectious.

Injury causes inflammation and fibrosis that impair ventilation and gas exchange. The scarring damages the alveoli, most often permanently, and the tissue becomes stiff and restrictive. That is why patients most commonly present with shortness of breath. Fibrosis is permanent scar tissue, a response to inflammation.

cards.t: How lung fibrosis develops: injury, inflammation, aberrant healing
q: how does pulmonary fibrosis develop
what is alveolitis
why do some lungs heal and others scar
cards.x:
Pulmonary fibrosis starts with injury. Exogenous and endogenous stimuli (dust, fumes, cigarette smoke, autoimmune conditions, drugs, infections, radiation) cause microscopic lung injury.

What happens next decides the outcome. If wound healing is intact, the lung returns to homeostasis (its normal balance). If healing is aberrant, which can reflect genetic predisposition or autoimmune conditions, the result is pulmonary fibrosis.

The cellular chain is: macrophages, lymphocytes, monocytes and neutrophils accumulate in the alveolar walls, producing alveolitis (inflammation of the air sacs). That drives fibroblasts to produce collagen, and the collagen is the fibrosis.

cards.t: Interstitial lung disease: known versus unknown causes
k: most common cause of interstitial lung disease
q: what are the most common known causes of interstitial lung disease
what are the most common unknown causes of interstitial lung disease
why take an occupational history in interstitial lung disease
cards.x:
Interstitial lung diseases fall into two groups, inflammation with fibrosis and granulomatous reactions, and each group is divided into known and unknown causes. Most have acute and chronic stages.

The most common known causes are occupational or environmental exposures: inorganic dusts, organic dusts, and fumes and gases. So take the occupational and exposure history, because it is the clue to the known causes.

The most common unknown (idiopathic) ones are sarcoidosis, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and pulmonary fibrosis with connective tissue disorders.

cards.t: Categories of interstitial lung disease by cause
q: how is interstitial lung disease classified
which diseases are idiopathic interstitial pneumonias
which interstitial lung diseases are granulomatous
cards.x:
A working classification of interstitial lung disease by cause:

- Known cause: occupational exposure (asbestosis, silicosis) and treatment-related (radiation, methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, chemotherapeutics).
- Systemic disease: connective tissue disease (rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, polymyositis and dermatomyositis).
- Unknown cause: the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, which are idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease, desquamative interstitial pneumonia, cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, acute interstitial pneumonia and lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia.
- Granulomatous lung disease: sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and with vasculitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and Churg-Strauss.
- Other: lymphangioleiomyomatosis, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis.

cards.t: Drug-induced and radiation-induced interstitial lung disease
q: which drugs cause interstitial lung disease
does methotrexate cause lung disease
what kind of picture suggests a drug cause of interstitial lung disease
cards.x:
Treatment-related interstitial lung disease has a short core list: radiation, methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin and chemotherapeutic drugs. Nitrofurantoin is also named among drugs that cause pulmonary toxicity.

The full list of drug causes is long and includes amphotericin B, bleomycin, busulfan, carbamazepine, chlorambucil, cocaine, cyclophosphamide, diphenylhydantoin, flecainide, heroin, melphalan, methadone, methylphenidate, methysergide, procarbazine and the vinca alkaloids (with mitomycin). Mineral oil causes it through chronic microaspiration, and silicone through subcutaneous injection.

A clinical picture of exertional dyspnea, dry cough, crackles and restriction after years of taking a drug such as nitrofurantoin fits a drug cause.

cards.t: Occupational and environmental exposures that cause lung fibrosis
q: what are inorganic versus organic dust exposures
which lung diseases come from inorganic dusts
which lung diseases come from organic dusts
cards.x:
Exposures are grouped as inorganic dusts, organic dusts, and fumes or gases.

- Inorganic examples: asbestosis, silicosis, coal workers' pneumoconiosis, berylliosis, aluminosis (from metallic aluminum powder), siderosis, talc pneumoconiosis, exposure to hard metals, and radiation fibrosis.
- Organic examples: farmer's lung, bird fancier's lung, hot tub lung, humidifier lung, bagassosis, mushroom worker's lung, malt worker's lung, coffee worker's lung and tea grower's lung.

Stone work releases free crystalline silica, so it is an inorganic dust exposure. Pneumoconiosis in general is caused by inhaled coal dust or various inorganic or silicate dusts.

cards.t: Interstitial lung disease: acute, subacute, chronic and episodic onset
k: acute vs chronic interstitial lung disease
q: how fast do interstitial lung diseases develop
which interstitial lung disease has an episodic pattern
which interstitial lung diseases are subacute
cards.x:
How quickly the illness develops is a clue to the cause:

- Acute: days to weeks, with allergy.
- Subacute: weeks to months. It can occur with any cause but is most common with sarcoidosis and drug-induced disease.
- Chronic: months to years. This is the pattern in most interstitial lung diseases, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis, pneumoconiosis and connective tissue disease.
- Episodic: less common, and seen with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, where inhaled organic material leads to illness after exposure. Symptoms can be reversible if the problem is caught early.

cards.t: Interstitial lung disease: symptoms and examination findings
q: what are the symptoms of interstitial lung disease
what does the lung exam show in interstitial lung disease
what signs mean interstitial lung disease is advanced
cards.x:
Symptoms: progressive exertional dyspnea or a persistent nonproductive cough. Other symptoms can include hemoptysis (coughing up blood), wheezing, chest pain, tachypnea (fast breathing) and anorexia. As the disease progresses, dyspnea appears at rest.

Examination: small lung volumes and bibasilar dry rales, which are inspiratory crackles at the lung bases, plus distal clubbing. Right heart failure appears with advanced disease. Early in the disease, though, the exam may be normal.

cards.t: Lab clues that point to a specific interstitial lung disease
q: which lab goes with which interstitial lung disease
what does an elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme mean
what does c-ANCA suggest in lung disease
cards.x:
Each abnormal lab test points toward a particular disease:

- Raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate: active sarcoidosis.
- High antinuclear antibody: collagen vascular diseases.
- Cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA): granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
- Anti-glomerular basement membrane and anti-alveolar basement membrane antibodies: Goodpasture syndrome, which is glomerulonephritis plus diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage, mostly in young adults.
- Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme: sarcoidosis.
- Eosinophilia: eosinophilic pneumonia, sarcoidosis or drug-induced disease.

A complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel give the baseline.

cards.t: Chest film patterns in interstitial lung disease
q: what do reticular opacities mean on a chest film
what does honeycombing mean
which interstitial lung diseases cause hilar lymphadenopathy
cards.x:
The chest film in interstitial lung disease shows low lung volumes and patchy opacities that can be ground-glass, reticular, nodular, reticulonodular or cystic. Hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy suggests sarcoidosis or silicosis.

Reading the pattern:

- Reticular (curvilinear) opacities: fine (ground glass) means early disease; medium (honeycombing) means late disease; coarse means cystic spaces.
- Nodular: nodules.
- Reticulonodular: reticular shadows overlapping nodules, as in sarcoidosis.

Going from ground glass to honeycombing marks progression of fibrosis. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, the brighter interstitial markings are in the lower lung fields.

cards.t: The restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing
q: what does a restrictive pattern look like on pulmonary function tests
why is the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity normal in interstitial lung disease
what are normal values for the ratio and forced vital capacity
cards.x:
Interstitial lung disease stiffens the lung so that it no longer expands well. That gives a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing: total lung capacity and forced vital capacity fall (normal is 80% or more of predicted), while the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity stays normal or rises (normal is 0.70 or more).

The key contrast is the ratio. In a restrictive pattern the lung volumes fall, but the ratio does not fall with them.

cards.t: Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias (the subtypes)
q: what are the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias
which idiopathic interstitial pneumonias are treated with corticosteroids
what is the most common idiopathic interstitial pneumonia
cards.x:
The idiopathic (fibrosing) interstitial pneumonias are interstitial pneumonias of unknown cause that are defined by their histopathologic (tissue) pattern. The patterns are idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, desquamative interstitial pneumonitis, nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease, lymphoid interstitial pneumonia and acute interstitial pneumonitis.

Suspect one in any unexplained interstitial lung disease. Together they are the most common diagnosis among patients with interstitial lung disease, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the most common subtype. Diagnosis may require a biopsy, with age, sex, prodrome, imaging and histology all weighed. Symptoms, treatment and prognosis all depend on the subtype. Corticosteroids may be used in cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia), lymphoid interstitial pneumonia and nonspecific interstitial pneumonia.

cards.t: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: what it is and how it presents
q: what is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
what are the symptoms of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
what does the exam show in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
cards.x:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the most common idiopathic (fibrosing) interstitial pneumonia, and the most common diagnosis among patients with interstitial lung disease. It is pulmonary fibrosis with the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern and no associated cause. The cause is listed as unknown, yet smoking is given as the cause in the majority of cases, and 67 to 75% of patients with it and familial lung fibrosis have a history of smoking.

Symptoms come on insidiously (slowly and quietly): a dry cough, exertional dyspnea, and constitutional symptoms such as fatigue and malaise.

Examination shows clubbing, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, tachypnea and reduced chest expansion.

cards.t: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: imaging, testing and management
q: what does idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis look like on CT
how is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis treated
does any treatment improve survival in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
cards.x:
The tests fit a scarring, stiff lung:

- Chest film: progressive fibrosis over several areas.
- Computed tomography (CT): diffuse patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing, meaning clustered small air spaces lining the lung edges.
- Pulmonary function: restrictive, with decreased lung volume and a normal to increased ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity.
- Bronchoalveolar lavage, transbronchial biopsy or surgical lung biopsy when needed.

Management is controversial. Nothing has been shown to improve survival or quality of life compared with no treatment, though an accurate diagnosis identifies who may benefit. Smoking is the cause in the majority of cases, and smoking cessation is critical to prolong life.

cards.t: Interstitial lung disease with connective tissue (autoimmune) disease
k: pulmonary fibrosis with connective tissue disease
q: which autoimmune diseases cause interstitial lung disease
how does connective tissue disease affect the lungs
can methotrexate cause interstitial lung disease
cards.x:
When the lung disease sits in a patient with a connective tissue disease, think autoimmune: an inflammatory and fibrotic response in the lungs. The diseases include systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, systemic sclerosis, Sjogren syndrome, polymyositis-dermatomyositis and scleroderma.

There is a drug twist: methotrexate, used to treat many autoimmune diseases including lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, is itself a cause of interstitial lung disease. So the lung disease can come from the autoimmune disease or from its treatment.

The usual features are chronic progressive exertional dyspnea and nonproductive cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, clubbing and small lung volumes. A high antinuclear antibody suggests collagen vascular disease, and pulmonary function is restrictive.

cards.t: Pulmonary hemorrhage syndromes and Goodpasture syndrome
q: what are the pulmonary hemorrhage syndromes
which antibody causes Goodpasture syndrome
what are alveolar filling disorders
cards.x:
The pulmonary hemorrhage syndromes, also called alveolar filling disorders, are bleeding into the air sacs. The three named conditions are Goodpasture syndrome, idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis and isolated pulmonary capillaritis.

The one to link to a test is Goodpasture syndrome, which has anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies.

cards.t: Granulomatous lung disease and granulomatous vasculitis
q: what is a granulomatous lung disease
which vasculitides are granulomatous
what is granulomatosis with polyangiitis
cards.x:
A granulomatous response is still interstitial lung disease of unknown cause. T lymphocytes, macrophages and epithelioid cells organize themselves into granulomas in the lung tissue (the parenchyma).

Examples are sarcoidosis and the granulomatous vasculitides: granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener, and positive for the cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) pattern, c-ANCA) and the allergic granulomatosis of Churg-Strauss.

cards.t: Sarcoidosis: what it is and who gets it
q: what is sarcoidosis
who gets sarcoidosis
what causes sarcoidosis
cards.x:
Sarcoidosis is a multi-organ disease of idiopathic (unknown) cause, with noncaseating granulomatous inflammation. It can affect the lungs, lymph nodes, eyes, skin, liver, spleen, salivary glands, heart and nervous system, but the lungs and lymphatic system are most often affected. Granulomatous lung inflammation is present in about 90%.

The thought is that environmental triggers (viral, bacterial, mycobacterial, inhaled agents, mold and mildew) act in a genetically predisposed person. It may reflect a lack of modulation of the immune response after the antigen is recognized.

Who: more common in North American Black people and Northern European white people, more often in women, with onset in the third and fourth decades.

cards.t: Sarcoidosis: symptoms and examination (lupus pernio, erythema nodosum)
q: what are the symptoms of sarcoidosis
what is lupus pernio
what skin findings occur in sarcoidosis
cards.x:
Sarcoidosis symptoms include cough, dyspnea of insidious onset, chest discomfort, malaise, fever, weakness and weight loss, plus nontender lymphadenopathy and signs from other organ systems.

On examination, look for:

- Erythema nodosum: itchy, painful rashes on the lower legs and ankles.
- Parotid enlargement.
- Lymph node, liver or spleen enlargement.
- Crackles in the lungs.
- Lupus pernio: painful skin sores on the face, a form of skin involvement.

The disease can also involve the eyes, heart and brain.

cards.t: Sarcoidosis: diagnosis, labs and biopsy
q: how is sarcoidosis diagnosed
what labs are abnormal in sarcoidosis
what does the chest film show in sarcoidosis
cards.x:
The chest film shows symmetric bilateral hilar and right paratracheal adenopathy and bilateral reticular infiltrates.

Labs: leukopenia, eosinophilia, an elevated sedimentation rate, hypercalcemia (about 5% of patients) and hypercalciuria (calcium in the urine). Angiotensin-converting enzyme is elevated in 40 to 80%.

Confirmation comes from a transbronchial lung biopsy or fine-needle node biopsy that shows noncaseating granulomas. Biopsy is essential whenever the clinical and radiographic findings suggest an alternative diagnosis such as lymphoma.

cards.t: Sarcoidosis chest film stages I to IV
q: what are the stages of sarcoidosis
what does stage II sarcoidosis show
which stage of sarcoidosis has the best prognosis
cards.x:
The chest film stages of sarcoidosis follow the lung involvement:

- Stage I: bilateral hilar adenopathy alone.
- Stage II: hilar adenopathy plus parenchymal involvement.
- Stage III: parenchymal involvement alone (diffuse reticular infiltrates).
- Stage IV: advanced fibrosis, with honeycombing, hilar retraction, bullae, cysts and emphysema.

The stage also links to prognosis. It is best with hilar adenopathy alone, and parenchymal involvement on imaging means a worse prognosis.

cards.t: Sarcoidosis treatment: corticosteroids and second-line drugs
q: how is sarcoidosis treated
when are corticosteroids used in sarcoidosis
what is used if sarcoidosis does not respond to steroids
cards.x:
About 90% of sarcoidosis responds to corticosteroids and can be controlled with moderate maintenance doses. Indications for oral corticosteroids include disabling constitutional symptoms, hypercalcemia, iritis, uveitis, arthritis, central nervous system involvement, cardiac involvement, granulomatous hepatitis, cutaneous lesions other than erythema nodosum, and progressive pulmonary lesions.

For patients who cannot tolerate corticosteroids, or whose disease is corticosteroid-refractory, immunosuppressants are used, most commonly methotrexate, azathioprine or infliximab.

A catch: methotrexate also treats autoimmune diseases such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, but it has been implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease. Azathioprine or infliximab covers the same refractory indication.

cards.t: Sarcoidosis prognosis and yearly follow-up
q: what is the prognosis of sarcoidosis
what follow-up do sarcoidosis patients need
how many sarcoidosis patients develop irreversible lung damage
cards.x:
Sarcoidosis has the best prognosis with hilar adenopathy alone, and parenchymal involvement on imaging means a worse one. About 20% of patients with lung involvement develop irreversible impairment: progressive fibrosis, bronchiectasis or cavitation.

Every year, patients get a physical examination, pulmonary function tests, a chest film, an electrocardiogram, a chemistry panel and an ophthalmologic (eye) evaluation to find and manage ocular inflammation.

cards.t: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis
q: what is coal workers' pneumoconiosis
what is simple versus complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis
what is progressive massive fibrosis
cards.x:
Pneumoconiosis is a chronic fibrotic lung disease from inhaling coal dust or various inorganic or silicate dusts. In coal workers' pneumoconiosis, alveolar macrophages take up the inhaled coal dust and form coal macules.

There are two forms. Simple disease is usually asymptomatic, with unimpressive pulmonary function. Complicated disease is progressive massive fibrosis, in which the lesions conglomerate (merge) and contract in the upper lungs. It brings dyspnea that keeps progressing, inspiratory crackles, finger clubbing and cyanosis.

cards.t: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis: tests and management
q: what does coal workers' pneumoconiosis look like on chest film
how is coal workers' pneumoconiosis treated
what do pulmonary function tests show in coal workers' pneumoconiosis
cards.x:
Tests: pulmonary function is restrictive with reduced diffusing capacity (the diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide). The chest film shows nodular opacities in the upper lung fields, the coal macules, 2 to 5 mm across.

There is no effective curative treatment, so management is supportive: oxygen, vaccinations (pneumococcal and influenza), rehabilitation and smoking cessation. Lung transplant is an option in severe cases. The complication to know is progressive massive fibrosis, conglomeration and contraction in the upper lung fields.

cards.t: Asbestosis: exposure, mechanism and symptoms
q: what is asbestosis
how does asbestos cause lung disease
how long after asbestos exposure does asbestosis appear
cards.x:
Asbestosis is lung scarring from asbestos fibers. The usual history is work in insulation, demolition, shipyards or construction, with exposure over 10 to 20 years. Patients usually seek attention about 15 years after exposure.

The mechanism is that asbestos invades lung tissue and cannot be removed. Chronic inflammation and macrophage invasion then scar the terminal bronchioles, alveoli and interstitium. Fibers can also penetrate further and cause mesothelioma.

Symptoms: dyspnea on exertion, rarely cough, and with progression fine bibasilar crackles and clubbing. A ferruginous body in tissue, a histologic finding resulting from inorganic dust inhalation, suggests significant exposure.

cards.t: Asbestosis: imaging and pulmonary function
q: what is the most common chest film finding in asbestosis
what imaging is preferred for asbestosis
what does pulmonary function show in asbestosis
cards.x:
Imaging is often normal early. Pleural plaques are the most common chest film finding (linear streaking at the bases), along with reticulonodular opacities at the bases. Computed tomography (CT) is the preferred imaging for asbestosis and shows pleural plaques, alveolitis and fibrosis, with honeycombing in advanced disease.

Labs are not helpful. Pulmonary function shows reduced vital capacity and total lung capacity.

cards.t: Asbestosis: management and complications
q: how is asbestosis treated
what are the complications of asbestosis
does smoking increase risk in asbestosis
cards.x:
Because the fibers cannot be removed, treatment is supportive: oxygen, physiotherapy, medications and vaccinations, along with smoking cessation.

The complications are an increased risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma, especially in smokers. Cigarette smoking increases radiographic pleural and parenchymal changes and markedly increases lung carcinoma.

cards.t: Mesothelioma
q: what is mesothelioma
what causes mesothelioma
is mesothelioma curable
cards.x:
Mesothelioma is primarily a cancer of the pleural lining and is nearly always caused by asbestos. Asbestos fibers can penetrate further into the lung and cause it, and asbestos workers have a 10% lifetime risk.

It is incurable, with poor long-term survival. No treatment is known to prolong survival, so care is primarily supportive. Pleural effusions are frequent, and the diagnosis can be made by pleural fluid cytology.

cards.t: Silicosis: exposure and mechanism
q: what is silicosis
who gets silicosis
why does silicosis affect the upper lobes
cards.x:
Silicosis is lung fibrosis from inhaling free crystalline silica dust (silicon dioxide). The history is mining, sandblasting, quarry work or stone work.

The silica deposits in the alveoli, causing chronic inflammation, macrophage invasion and fibrosis, and it also makes nodular lesions. It is usually carried to the upper lobes because it is a lighter dust.

As with coal workers' pneumoconiosis, there is a simple form that is usually asymptomatic with unimpressive function, and a complicated form with conglomeration of the upper lungs.

cards.t: Silicosis: symptoms and tests
q: what are the symptoms of silicosis
what does bronchoalveolar lavage show in silicosis
what do labs show in silicosis
cards.x:
Silicosis presents with dyspnea, cough, weight loss and fatigue, and often crackles.

Labs are mostly not contributory, apart from an arterial blood gas. Pulmonary function shows reduced forced vital capacity and reduced forced expiratory volume in 1 second.

The distinctive test is bronchoalveolar lavage (washing out the airways to collect fluid), which returns a thick, milky effluent with foamy, lipoproteinaceous macrophages.

cards.t: Silicosis on imaging: silicotic nodules and eggshell calcification
q: what does silicosis look like on chest film
what is eggshell calcification
how big are silicotic nodules
cards.x:
Silicosis shows nodular opacities throughout the lungs. These are silicotic nodules, 1 to 10 mm across, which make up a nodular pulmonary fibrosis. The classic extra finding is eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes: the nodes show a thin bright rim around them.

These findings together with a history of mining, sandblasting, quarry work or stone work point to silicosis.

cards.t: Silicosis: complications and management
q: what are the complications of silicosis
why do silicosis patients get a tuberculosis skin test
how is silicosis treated
cards.x:
Silicosis is treated largely with supportive care: oxygen, physiotherapy, medications and vaccinations, plus smoking cessation.

The complications are an increased risk of tuberculosis, progressive massive fibrosis and scleroderma. Because of the tuberculosis risk, patients should have a tuberculosis skin test and a current chest film. Scleroderma is also one of the connective tissue diseases that cause interstitial lung disease.

cards.t: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: what it is and what causes it
q: what is hypersensitivity pneumonitis
what causes hypersensitivity pneumonitis
why is prompt diagnosis important in hypersensitivity pneumonitis
cards.x:
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (also called extrinsic allergic alveolitis) is a non-atopic, non-asthmatic inflammatory lung disease in which inhaled organic material causes illness. The sources are moldy hay, bird excreta and feathers, moldy sugarcane pulp, other moldy products and insect-infested grain. The named versions are bird fancier's lung, farmer's lung and cheese maker's lung.

The key is prompt diagnosis, because the fix is to remove the patient from the environment. Symptoms can reverse if the disease is caught early, and continued exposure worsens it.

cards.t: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: acute, subacute and chronic forms
q: what are the symptoms of hypersensitivity pneumonitis
how soon after exposure do symptoms start in hypersensitivity pneumonitis
what is chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis
cards.x:
In the acute form, symptoms start 4 to 8 hours after exposure (the acute form is listed as within 9 hours of exposure): sudden malaise, chills, fever, cough, dyspnea and nausea, a flu-like illness with rales. It may mimic paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea because it hits after work, once the person is home. Exam shows bibasilar crackles, tachypnea, tachycardia and cyanosis.

The subacute (15%) and chronic (5%) forms follow multiple exposures:

- Subacute: rales, cough, chronic bronchitis, shortness of breath, anorexia or weight loss.
- Chronic: cough, chronic bronchitis, shortness of breath, anorexia or weight loss, plus fatigue, lung fibrosis and clubbing.

Only the acute form has the flu-like illness, and only the chronic form has fatigue, fibrosis and clubbing.

cards.t: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: tests and findings
q: how is hypersensitivity pneumonitis diagnosed
what does hypersensitivity pneumonitis look like on CT
what does the biopsy show in hypersensitivity pneumonitis
cards.x:
Several tests fit hypersensitivity pneumonitis:

- Antibodies to the agent in the serum: their presence gives a definitive diagnosis.
- Blood: white count elevated with a left shift, and hypoxia.
- Imaging: chest film and computed tomography (CT) show little change acutely. In subacute and chronic disease there are fibrotic changes and small nodular densities that spare the apices and bases.
- Pulmonary function: restrictive.
- Biopsy: may be indicated in subacute or chronic disease. Histology shows interstitial lymphocytes and plasma cells with non-caseating granulomas.

cards.t: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis treatment: find the agent, avoid the agent
q: how is hypersensitivity pneumonitis treated
what is the most important treatment for hypersensitivity pneumonitis
when are corticosteroids used in hypersensitivity pneumonitis
cards.x:
The first step is to identify the agent responsible, and the second is to avoid it. Everything else supports that. Corticosteroids are used in severe cases, and other immunosuppressants are an option. Supportive care includes oxygen, bronchodilators and pain medications, and lung transplant is also listed.

This works because the disease can be reversed when it is caught early, while continued exposure makes it worse and can lead to fibrosis.

cards.t: ARDS (acute respiratory distress syndrome): definition and diagnostic criteria
q: what is acute respiratory distress syndrome
what are the criteria for diagnosing acute respiratory distress syndrome
how is acute respiratory distress syndrome different from heart failure
cards.x:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is acute, non-cardiogenic lung injury. The criteria are:

- Timing: it develops within 7 days of a known clinical insult.
- Imaging: bilateral pulmonary opacities not explained by effusion, atelectasis or nodules.
- Origin: non-cardiogenic, meaning the respiratory failure is not fully explained by heart failure or fluid overload.
- Oxygenation: the ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to the fraction of inspired oxygen is under 300 mm Hg (or oxygen saturation to inspired fraction under 315).

About one-third of cases first present with sepsis.

cards.t: ARDS severity: the arterial oxygen to inspired oxygen ratio
q: how is ARDS severity graded
how do you calculate the arterial oxygen to inspired oxygen ratio
what ratio means severe ARDS
cards.x:
Severity of acute respiratory distress syndrome is graded by dividing the arterial oxygen pressure (in mm Hg) by the fraction of inspired oxygen, a ratio that tells you how well the lungs are getting oxygen into the blood. A lower ratio is worse:

- Mild: 200 to 300 mm Hg.
- Moderate: 100 to 200 mm Hg.
- Severe: under 100 mm Hg.

Worked example: an arterial oxygen of 60 mm Hg on 50% oxygen (a fraction of 0.5) gives 60 divided by 0.5, which is 120. That is moderate.

cards.t: Causes of ARDS: direct pulmonary versus systemic
q: what causes acute respiratory distress syndrome
what are direct versus systemic causes of ARDS
can drugs cause ARDS
cards.x:
Causes split into insults that hit the lung directly and insults that start elsewhere in the body.

- Direct pulmonary: aspiration of gastric contents, diffuse pneumonia, lung contusion, toxic gas (chlorine, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, ammonia, smoke), near-drowning, high altitude, radiation, upper airway obstruction, and fat, air, amniotic fluid or thrombus emboli.
- Systemic: sepsis, severe pancreatitis, shock, nonthoracic trauma, overdoses (opioids, aspirin, phenothiazine, tricyclic antidepressants, cocaine), multiple blood transfusions, disseminated intravascular coagulation, cardiopulmonary bypass, protamine, and chemotherapy, amiodarone or nitrofurantoin.

Sepsis is the one to watch: about one-third of cases first present with it.

cards.t: ARDS mechanism: inflammation, leaky capillaries and refractory hypoxemia
q: why does ARDS cause severe hypoxemia
what happens in the lungs in ARDS
what is the hyperinflammatory phenotype of ARDS
cards.x:
In acute respiratory distress syndrome, pro-inflammatory cytokines damage the capillary endothelium and the alveolar epithelium. Vascular permeability increases, which leads to surfactant loss and alveolar collapse. The end result is refractory hypoxemia, low oxygen that does not respond to extra oxygen.

A hyperinflammatory phenotype, with high interleukin-6 and soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor, correlates with multiorgan failure and higher mortality.

cards.t: ARDS presentation, imaging and differential diagnosis
q: what are the symptoms of ARDS
what does the chest film show in ARDS
how do you tell ARDS from cardiogenic pulmonary edema
cards.x:
Presentation: profound dyspnea 12 to 48 hours after the insult, with tachypnea, labored breathing, intercostal retractions and crackles. The hypoxemia is marked and refractory to supplemental oxygen, and multiple organ failure can follow (kidneys, liver, gut, central nervous system, cardiovascular).

Imaging: bilateral infiltrates rapidly progress to confluent opacities, with air bronchograms in about 80%. The heart size is normal, with minimal or absent pleural effusions. Echocardiography assesses cardiac function to exclude hydrostatic (cardiogenic) pulmonary edema.

Differential: cardiogenic pulmonary edema (cardiomegaly, vascular engorgement, batwing perihilar opacities), diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, severe bilateral pneumonia and autoimmune lung disease.

cards.t: ARDS management: ventilation, positioning and treating the cause
q: how is ARDS treated with the ventilator
does prone positioning help ARDS
should high-frequency oscillatory ventilation be used in ARDS
cards.x:
Management starts with treating the primary precipitant promptly. Then:

- Use low tidal volumes.
- Titrate positive end-expiratory pressure to keep arterial oxygen above 60 mm Hg.
- Use early prone positioning (lying face down), which decreases mortality in moderate to severe disease.
- Avoid high-frequency oscillatory ventilation, because there is no proven benefit.

cards.t: ARDS management: fluids, transfusion, drugs and salvage therapy
q: how should fluids be managed in ARDS
when do you transfuse in ARDS
when is extracorporeal membrane oxygenation used in ARDS
cards.x:
Fluids and blood: use conservative fluids. A central venous pressure target under 4 mm Hg is used, and restrictive fluids increase ventilator-free days and shorten intensive care stays. Avoid routine pulmonary artery catheters (no clinical benefit). Transfuse at hemoglobin 7 g/dL, since higher targets do not improve outcomes, and avoid supranormal oxygen delivery targets.

Drugs and salvage: corticosteroids are conditionally supported within 14 days. Sedatives, analgesics and antipyretics reduce oxygen demand. Neuromuscular blockade is controversial because mortality data conflict. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is for severe, refractory disease.

cards.t: ARDS prognosis and recovery
q: what is the mortality of ARDS
what determines survival in ARDS
do patients recover lung function after ARDS
cards.x:
Overall mortality is about 30% with low tidal volume ventilation, but the cause drives survival: about 20% mortality after trauma versus 80% with end-stage liver disease.

Lung function generally recovers within 6 to 12 months, though functional deficits often remain. Residual diffusion deficits and obstructive changes often persist. Survivors may also have post-intensive care muscle wasting, weakness and fatigue, and treating these physical effects is part of recovery.

cards.t: Supportive care and follow-up across inflammatory lung diseases
q: what supportive care do chronic lung disease patients need
who needs a lung transplant in inflammatory lung disease
what follow-up is needed in sarcoidosis and silicosis
cards.x:
Most of the chronic occupational lung diseases share the same supportive care: oxygen, vaccinations (pneumococcal and influenza), rehabilitation and physiotherapy, and smoking cessation. Lung transplant is for severe pneumoconiosis or hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

Follow-up depends on the disease. In sarcoidosis, patients get a yearly exam, pulmonary function tests, chest film, electrocardiogram, chemistry panel and eye examination. In silicosis, they get a tuberculosis skin test and a current chest film. Survivors of acute respiratory distress syndrome recover lung function over 6 to 12 months, with residual diffusion deficits and post-intensive-care weakness.

The occupational and environmental history identifies the known causes, and drugs such as methotrexate, amiodarone and nitrofurantoin are also on that list.
